summary: SNRI that’s FDA-approved for fibromyalgia—not depression. In psychiatry it’s sometimes used off-label for major depression, but it comes with the standard antidepressant suicidality warning (especially ages 18–24) and can raise blood pressure and heart rate.
description: Milnacipran (Savella) is an SNRI that increases serotonin and norepinephrine. In the US it’s approved for fibromyalgia, but psychiatrists may see it used off-label for depression. Like other antidepressants, it can temporarily increase suicidal thinking/behavior in some younger people early in treatment or after dose changes, so close monitoring matters. It can also cause nausea, insomnia, sweating, sexual side effects, and increases in blood pressure or pulse.
patient_summary: Milnacipran (Savella) is an SNRI. It’s not FDA-approved for depression in the US, but some clinicians use it off-label. Early on (or after a dose change), some people feel more keyed up, restless, or more suicidal—especially ages 18–24—so you don’t “set it and forget it.” It can also cause nausea, insomnia, sweating, sexual side effects, and higher blood pressure/heart rate.

secondary.context: Like other antidepressants, starting milnacipran (or changing the dose) can be associated with new or worsening suicidal thinking/behavior in some patients—highest concern in children, adolescents, and young adults (18–24). Close monitoring is a must.

SNRIs can reduce anxiety in some people, but they can also rev up anxiety, restlessness, or insomnia early in treatment. If anxiety or agitation spikes after starting or increasing the dose, the plan may need to change.

off_label.context: Milnacipran is not FDA-approved for major depressive disorder (MDD) in the US, but it is sometimes used off-label as an SNRI option when other antidepressants aren’t a fit or haven’t worked.

therapeutic_response.display: Not a fast-acting sedative; antidepressant effects (when used off-label) typically build over days to weeks

common_adverse_effects.notes: This is the big one. Taking it with food and titrating more slowly can help. It often improves over time, but if it’s persistent or severe, dose changes or a different medication may be a better move.
Hydration, fiber, and routine movement matter here. If constipation is severe, don’t just suffer—tell your clinician.
Headaches can show up early and sometimes fade as your body adjusts. If headaches are intense or persistent, it’s worth re-checking blood pressure and dose timing.

Milnacipran can be activating for some people. If sleep gets worse, your prescriber may adjust timing, slow the titration, or reconsider the medication—especially if insomnia triggers anxiety or suicidal thinking.
Dizziness can happen during titration. Stand up slowly, stay hydrated, and let your clinician know if you’re having near-fainting or falls.
Heat/sweating symptoms are a common SNRI vibe. If you’re also having agitation, tremor, diarrhea, fever, or confusion, that’s a different story—think serotonin syndrome and get help.

serious_risks.risk: Suicidal thinking/behavior (highest concern in ages 18–24 early in treatment or after dose changes): urgent evaluation needed if worsening
Mania/hypomania: decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, impulsivity, grandiosity—especially if bipolar risk
Serotonin syndrome: agitation, confusion, sweating, tremor, diarrhea, fever, muscle rigidity (medical emergency)
Hypertensive crisis or sustained hypertension/tachycardia: severe headache, chest pain, shortness of breath, neurologic symptoms (medical emergency)
Severe skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome/erythema multiforme): blistering rash, mucosal involvement (medical emergency)
Hyponatremia/SIADH: confusion, severe headache, weakness, seizures (medical emergency)
Seizures (rare but reported; higher risk with predisposition)
Severe urinary retention (painful inability to urinate, distended bladder): urgent evaluation

safety.black_box_warning: Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thinking and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults (18 to 24) in short-term studies of major depressive disorder and other psychiatric disorders. Closely monitor for clinical worsening, suicidality, or unusual changes in behavior, especially during the first months of therapy and after dose changes. Milnacipran is not approved for treatment of major depressive disorder in the US and is not approved for pediatric patients.

contraindications.contraindication: Use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) intended to treat psychiatric disorders (concurrently or within 5 days of discontinuing milnacipran, or within 2 weeks of discontinuing the MAOI)
Initiation of milnacipran in a patient receiving IV methylene blue

precautions: Activation symptoms can happen early: anxiety, agitation, panic attacks, insomnia, irritability, hostility, impulsivity, akathisia, hypomania, or mania
Serotonin syndrome is rare but potentially life-threatening—risk rises when combined with other serotonergic meds
Blood pressure and heart rate can increase; sustained hypertension or tachycardia may require dose reduction or discontinuation
Bleeding risk may increase, especially with NSAIDs, aspirin, anticoagulants, or other agents that affect clotting
Urinary hesitation/retention can occur (higher concern in people with prostate issues or baseline urinary problems)
May precipitate mania/hypomania in people with bipolar disorder; screen before treating depressive symptoms

interactions.interactant: MAOIs (psychiatric MAOIs; also IV methylene blue)
interactions.mechanism: Contraindicated due to serotonin syndrome risk (potentially life-threatening).
interactions.action: Do not combine. Allow at least 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting milnacipran. Allow at least 5 days between stopping milnacipran and starting an MAOI.

interactions.interactant: Other serotonergic agents (SSRIs/SNRIs, TCAs, triptans, fentanyl, lithium, tramadol, buspirone, amphetamines, St. John’s wort, tryptophan, methadone, meperidine)
interactions.action: Use caution and monitor closely. Educate on serotonin syndrome symptoms and stop the drug(s) and seek urgent care if symptoms appear.

interactions.interactant: NSAIDs/aspirin/anticoagulants (warfarin) and other drugs that affect clotting
interactions.mechanism: Increased bleeding risk due to impaired platelet aggregation.
interactions.action: Use caution, especially if there’s a history of GI bleeding or you’re on multiple agents that increase bleeding risk. Monitor for bruising, nosebleeds, black stools, or unusual bleeding.

interactions.interactant: Medications that raise blood pressure/heart rate (some stimulants, decongestants, certain activating agents)
interactions.mechanism: Additive increases in BP/HR; higher risk in people with hypertension or tachyarrhythmias.
interactions.action: Monitor BP/HR and reconsider combinations if BP/pulse climbs or symptoms develop.

interactions.mechanism: Traditionally listed as contraindicated due to serotonin syndrome concerns; emerging evidence suggests low absolute risk in many scenarios, but monitoring is required.
interactions.action: If combination is necessary, monitor carefully for serotonin toxicity and educate the patient on symptoms; risk may increase with longer overlapping durations.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Suicidal ideation and behavior: monitor closely at the beginning of therapy and after dose increases or decreases, especially in ages 18–24; watch for sudden behavior changes and clinical worsening
Mood activation: anxiety, agitation, insomnia, irritability, impulsivity, akathisia, hypomania/mania; screen for bipolar disorder if depressive symptoms present
Blood pressure and heart rate: check baseline and periodically; consider dose reduction or discontinuation if sustained hypertension or tachycardia develops
Serotonin syndrome: monitor for agitation, confusion, diaphoresis, tremor, diarrhea, fever—especially with serotonergic combinations
Hyponatremia/SIADH risk: consider sodium monitoring in older adults and those on diuretics or with volume depletion; monitor for confusion, weakness, headaches
Renal function: monitor for dosing purposes, especially in older adults and those with known kidney disease
Ocular effects: monitor intraocular pressure in those with baseline elevations or glaucoma risk; watch for narrow-angle glaucoma symptoms
Sexual function: ask directly before and during treatment; assess for libido changes, orgasm changes, erectile/ejaculatory problems
Urinary symptoms: hesitancy, retention, decreased output; higher concern in patients with prostate/lower urinary tract issues
Bleeding risk: monitor for bruising, epistaxis, GI bleeding signs when combined with NSAIDs/aspirin/anticoagulants

special_populations.pregnancy: Human data are insufficient to define risk. SNRI exposure in the third trimester can be associated with neonatal adaptation syndrome (usually resolves within 2 weeks) and has been associated with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (rare). SNRIs may increase bleeding risk and may be associated with postpartum hemorrhage when used close to delivery. For patients who are pregnant or planning pregnancy, decisions should be individualized and made with shared decision-making; if initiating an SNRI in pregnancy, start at half the lowest recommended dose and titrate gradually over 4 to 10 days, using the lowest effective single agent when possible.
special_populations.lactation: Milnacipran is present in human milk. Limited data (single-dose 50 mg in lactating women ≥12 weeks postpartum) estimate infant exposure around 5% of the maternal dose. Monitor infants for agitation, irritability, poor feeding, and poor weight gain. The decision to breastfeed during treatment should weigh infant exposure risk, the benefits of breastfeeding, and the benefits of maternal treatment.
special_populations.pediatric: Not approved for pediatric patients and not approved for pediatric depression treatment.
special_populations.geriatric: Use caution in adults ≥65. SNRIs are flagged as potentially inappropriate to use with caution due to SIADH/hyponatremia risk; monitor sodium closely when initiating or adjusting doses. Older adults may also have higher exposure due to reduced renal function.
special_populations.renal_impairment: Mild impairment: no adjustment typically needed. Moderate impairment: use with caution. Severe impairment (CrCl ≤29): reduce maintenance to 25 mg twice daily; may increase to 50 mg twice daily if tolerated. ESRD: not recommended.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: No dosage adjustment generally necessary even in severe impairment based on single-dose data; use caution. Manufacturer suggests generally avoiding use in patients with substantial ethanol intake or evidence of chronic liver disease (risk factors for drug-induced liver injury).

pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Can be taken with or without food; food may improve tolerability

dosing.titration: Milnacipran is dosed with a starter titration when used for fibromyalgia. In psychiatry, if it’s used off-label for depression, dosing is typically started low and increased based on response and tolerability. Because this can be activating for some people (and because of suicidality monitoring early on), the goal is steady, deliberate titration—not rushing.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: If you’ve been on milnacipran for more than a few weeks, don’t stop abruptly. Antidepressant discontinuation can feel awful and can also make it harder to tell whether symptoms are withdrawal or relapse. The safest move is a planned taper.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Savella is FDA-approved for fibromyalgia. In psychiatry, milnacipran may show up off-label for {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:major depressive disorder}, but it’s important to know it’s not FDA-approved for depression in the US and it carries the same suicidality warning as other antidepressants—especially early in treatment and in younger people.

Mood + pain overlap: Considered occasionally when depression and chronic pain features are tangled together (clinical judgment varies)

My sleep got lighter and I was waking up more.
I felt a little restless and irritable until things leveled out.
items.note: Some people feel more anxious, agitated, or insomnia-y early on (or after dose increases). If that happens, it deserves a check-in—especially if suicidal thoughts increase.

quotes: The nausea was real at first, but taking it with food helped.
My stomach felt off for a couple weeks, then improved.
Constipation surprised me more than I expected.
items.note: GI side effects are common and often improve with slower titration and taking doses with food.

items.category: Energy, focus, and mood over time
quotes: After a few weeks, my mood felt less heavy and more even.
I didn’t feel sedated—more like I could get moving again.
It wasn’t instant, but I noticed I could function better day-to-day.
items.note: If used off-label for depression, benefit (when it happens) usually builds over weeks, not hours.

quotes: It helped my mood, but I had to dial in timing or I couldn’t sleep.
If I took it too late, bedtime was a fight.
I felt more awake—good in the morning, not great at night.
items.note: Because it can be activating, dose timing matters. If insomnia is a problem, clinicians may adjust when it’s taken or slow the titration.

items.category: Sexual side effects and urination issues
quotes: My libido dropped and it was harder to finish.
I noticed urinary hesitation that I hadn’t had before.
items.note: Sexual dysfunction and urinary hesitation/retention can happen—bring it up early so the plan can be adjusted.

sections.intro: Not everyone experiences this the same way, but here’s the common “real life” pattern clinicians hear about:

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Milnacipran isn’t a “take it and feel calm in 30 minutes” medication. It’s an SNRI—effects are gradual.
key_points: 2–4 hours: Peak blood levels after a dose
Days to weeks: When used off-label for depression, symptom improvement (if it occurs) builds over time
6–8 hours: Average half-life (one reason it’s commonly dosed twice daily)
Dose changes matter: Side effects and mood shifts can show up after starting, increasing, or decreasing the dose

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Milnacipran is FDA-approved for fibromyalgia, not depression. When psychiatrists use it off-label for MDD, expectations are similar to other SNRIs: a gradual shift over weeks, with early side effects sometimes showing up before benefits. If there’s no meaningful improvement after an adequate trial at a tolerable dose, the plan usually shifts (optimize dose, switch, or augment).
sections.clinical_details: Off-label antidepressant dosing strategies commonly start low and titrate based on tolerability, watching closely for activation, insomnia, blood pressure/heart rate increases, serotonin syndrome risk with interacting drugs, and any emergence or worsening of suicidal thinking—especially during the first weeks and after dose changes.

sections.highlight: If suicidal thoughts get worse, agitation spikes, or behavior changes suddenly—especially early in treatment—treat that as urgent and contact your prescriber right away.

patient_counseling: Watch for mood or behavior changes that feel “not you,” especially early on: worsening depression, new suicidal thoughts, agitation, restlessness, insomnia, or risky/impulsive behavior.
If suicidal thoughts increase, don’t white-knuckle it—call your prescriber urgently. If you feel at imminent risk, call 988 (US) or emergency services.
Tell your clinician about any bipolar history (or family history), seizure history, glaucoma risk, urinary problems, and your full med/supplement list.
Check blood pressure and pulse as recommended—especially if you already have hypertension or a fast heart rate.
Don’t stop suddenly if you’ve been on it for weeks—tapering reduces withdrawal symptoms.

sections.intro: Milnacipran interacts most dangerously with MAOIs and other serotonergic medications. It can also raise bleeding risk with certain meds and increase blood pressure/pulse alongside stimulatory agents.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If you’ve been on milnacipran for more than a few weeks, don’t stop abruptly. Antidepressant discontinuation can feel awful and can also make it harder to tell whether symptoms are withdrawal or relapse. The safest move is a planned taper.
key_points: If treatment lasted ≥4 weeks: taper gradually over about 2 to 4 weeks to minimize withdrawal symptoms and watch for returning symptoms.
If brief treatment (2 to 3 weeks): taper over 1 to 2 weeks may be reasonable.
If treatment <2 weeks: taper often isn’t necessary, but individual sensitivity varies.
Go slower (≥4 weeks, sometimes longer) if you’ve had withdrawal before or you were on higher doses.
Long-term treatment (>6 months): some patients do best with very slow tapers that extend beyond 3 months—especially if discontinuation syndrome has happened before.
If withdrawal symptoms become intolerable: return to the prior dose and taper more gradually.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Milnacipran is dosed with a starter titration when used for fibromyalgia. In psychiatry, if it’s used off-label for depression, dosing is typically started low and increased based on response and tolerability. Because this can be activating for some people (and because of suicidality monitoring early on), the goal is steady, deliberate titration—not rushing.

adult.mdd_off_label_initial: 25 to 50 mg PO twice daily (some experts start 25 mg PO once daily, then 25 mg PO twice daily on day 2, and if tolerated increase to 50 mg PO twice daily by day 7)
adult.mdd_off_label_titration: After 2 to 4 weeks, based on response and tolerability, may increase up to 100 mg PO twice daily; once at steady state (about 2 to 3 days after the last dose change), the total daily dose can sometimes be given once daily
adult.renal_severe_adjustment: If CrCl ≤29 mL/minute: reduce maintenance to 25 mg PO twice daily; may increase to 50 mg PO twice daily based on tolerance
adult.hepatic: No dosage adjustment generally necessary; use caution, and manufacturer suggests generally avoiding use in patients with substantial ethanol intake or evidence of chronic liver disease
adult.older_adult: Refer to adult dosing; use caution due to higher exposure with age-related renal decline and higher hyponatremia/SIADH risk

sections.simple_explanation: This isn’t a PRN med. If it’s used for depression off-label, you take it consistently and judge progress over weeks. Early side effects can show up before benefits, so dose increases should be paced to what your body can handle.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Pregnancy and breastfeeding decisions with SNRIs are about balancing risks: untreated mental health symptoms carry their own pregnancy risks, and stopping an effective medication can trigger relapse. Milnacipran also has limited human pregnancy safety data, and for fibromyalgia specifically many guidelines recommend maximizing nonmedication therapies before and during pregnancy.
sections.pregnancy: Human data are insufficient to define risk. SNRI exposure in the third trimester can be associated with neonatal adaptation syndrome (usually resolves within 2 weeks) and has been associated with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (rare). SNRIs may increase bleeding risk and may be associated with postpartum hemorrhage when used close to delivery. For patients who are pregnant or planning pregnancy, decisions should be individualized and made with shared decision-making; if initiating an SNRI in pregnancy, start at half the lowest recommended dose and titrate gradually over 4 to 10 days, using the lowest effective single agent when possible.
sections.lactation: Milnacipran is present in human milk. Limited data (single-dose 50 mg in lactating women ≥12 weeks postpartum) estimate infant exposure around 5% of the maternal dose. Monitor infants for agitation, irritability, poor feeding, and poor weight gain. The decision to breastfeed during treatment should weigh infant exposure risk, the benefits of breastfeeding, and the benefits of maternal treatment.
sections.pediatrics: Not approved for pediatric patients and not approved for pediatric depression treatment.
sections.geriatrics: Use caution in adults ≥65. SNRIs are flagged as potentially inappropriate to use with caution due to SIADH/hyponatremia risk; monitor sodium closely when initiating or adjusting doses. Older adults may also have higher exposure due to reduced renal function.
sections.hepatic: No dosage adjustment generally necessary even in severe impairment based on single-dose data; use caution. Manufacturer suggests generally avoiding use in patients with substantial ethanol intake or evidence of chronic liver disease (risk factors for drug-induced liver injury).
sections.renal: Mild impairment: no adjustment typically needed. Moderate impairment: use with caution. Severe impairment (CrCl ≤29): reduce maintenance to 25 mg twice daily; may increase to 50 mg twice daily if tolerated. ESRD: not recommended.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Savella is available as tablets and as a titration pack that helps you ramp up the dose more gently at the start.
items: Savella tablets: 12.5 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg (oral)
Savella Titration Pack: 12.5 mg + 25 mg + 50 mg tablets (starter pack)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Milnacipran is an SNRI: it blocks reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin (roughly 3:1 norepinephrine to serotonin). Translation: it increases those neurotransmitters in synapses, which can shift pain signaling and (off-label) depressive symptoms over time. It doesn’t meaningfully bind to histamine, muscarinic, dopamine, benzodiazepine, opiate, or GABA receptors and it’s not an MAOI.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: In psychiatry, milnacipran is not a first-line antidepressant in the US because it isn’t FDA-approved for MDD. If used off-label, it functions like an SNRI option when standard first-line antidepressants aren’t tolerated, aren’t effective, or when clinicians want an SNRI-style approach while keeping a close eye on activation, sleep disruption, blood pressure/pulse, and suicidality—especially early on. It is not a go-to sedating agent, and it’s not a PRN anxiety medication.

faqs.a: Mechanism-wise, yes—it’s an SNRI. But in the US, milnacipran is FDA-approved for fibromyalgia, not major depressive disorder. In psychiatry it may be used off-label for depression, but it’s not an FDA-approved depression med here.

faqs.q: Does Savella help anxiety or does it make it worse?
faqs.a: It can go either way. Some people feel less depressed and less anxious over time. But early on (or after dose increases) SNRIs can feel activating—more restlessness, insomnia, irritability, or “wired” anxiety. If anxiety ramps up, especially with suicidal thoughts, you should contact your prescriber quickly.

faqs.q: How long does milnacipran take to work for mood?
faqs.a: If it’s used off-label for depression, it usually works like other antidepressants: gradual improvement over days to weeks, not instant relief. Side effects like nausea or insomnia can show up before benefits.

faqs.q: What’s the biggest side effect to expect?
faqs.a: Nausea is the most common. Constipation, headache, insomnia, dizziness, sweating, and hot flashes are also common. Taking it with food and titrating more slowly can improve tolerability for many people.

faqs.q: What’s the suicidality warning with milnacipran?
faqs.a: Like other antidepressants, it can increase suicidal thinking/behavior compared with placebo in children, adolescents, and young adults (18–24) in short-term studies. The risk wasn’t increased in adults older than 24, and it was reduced in adults 65 and older. Regardless of age, everyone starting it should be monitored closely for clinical worsening, suicidality, or unusual behavior changes—especially early in treatment and after dose changes.

faqs.q: Can I take milnacipran with an MAOI?
faqs.a: No—this is a major contraindication. You generally need at least 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting milnacipran, and at least 5 days between stopping milnacipran and starting an MAOI.

faqs.q: Can milnacipran raise blood pressure or heart rate?
faqs.a: Yes. It can increase both blood pressure and pulse. That’s why clinicians check baseline vitals and monitor periodically. If sustained hypertension or tachycardia develops, the dose may need to be reduced or the medication tapered off.

faqs.q: Does Savella cause sexual side effects?
faqs.a: It can. Like other SNRIs, it may cause decreased libido and problems with orgasm. In men it can also cause erectile dysfunction or ejaculatory delay/failure. If this shows up, it’s fixable in many cases—dose changes, timing changes, or switching meds are all options.

If you’ve been on it for weeks, stopping suddenly can trigger discontinuation symptoms (nausea, dizziness, headaches, sweating, sleep disruption, anxiety, irritability, ‘electric shock’ sensations). A planned taper is usually the safest route—often over 2–4 weeks, sometimes longer if you’re sensitive or have been on it for months.

faqs.q: Is Savella sedating? Can it be used for sleep?
faqs.a: Usually no. Milnacipran is more likely to be activating than sedating, and insomnia is a common side effect. It’s not an insomnia medication and it’s not a PRN calm-down med.

faqs.q: Is milnacipran safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Human pregnancy data are limited. Like other SNRIs, late-pregnancy exposure can be associated with neonatal adaptation symptoms, and rare persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn has been reported with SNRIs as a class. Milnacipran is present in breast milk; infants should be monitored for irritability, poor feeding, and poor weight gain. Decisions should be individualized with shared decision-making that weighs the risks of untreated illness against medication exposure.
